cards.info: What is the formal definition of the second derivative $f''(x)$?
cards.backInfo: The second derivative $f''(x)$ is defined as the derivative of the first derivative $f'(x)$.

cards.info: In a motion model, what physical quantity does the second derivative of position represent?
cards.backInfo: The second derivative of position with respect to time represents acceleration.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A linear sequence showing the progression from position to jerk via differentiation.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/57543f47-142a-428d-a83e-914b337bc3ac-1786519342215-423.webp)

cards.info: What physical concept is represented by the third derivative of position with respect to time?
cards.backInfo: The third derivative of position with respect to time represents jerk.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A linear sequence showing the progression from position to jerk via differentiation.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/57543f47-142a-428d-a83e-914b337bc3ac-1786519342215-423.webp)

cards.info: How do units change with each successive differentiation with respect to time $t$?
cards.backInfo: Each differentiation adds a factor of $1/t$ to the units, such as changing meters to meters per second.

cards.info: True or False: If a particle's velocity is zero, its acceleration must also be zero.
cards.backInfo: False. A particle can be momentarily at rest while still having a non-zero acceleration.

cards.info: What does a negative second derivative $f''(x) < 0$ imply about the first derivative?
cards.backInfo: A negative second derivative indicates that the first derivative $f'(x)$ is decreasing at that point.

cards.info: What formula estimates $f''(a)$ using velocity values $v(a+h)$ and $v(a-h)$ from a table?
cards.backInfo: The finite-difference estimate is calculated using the symmetric difference quotient: $[v(a+h) - v(a-h)] / (2h)$.

cards.info: What is the correct Leibniz notation for the second derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$?
cards.backInfo: The correct notation is $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$.

cards.info: If a particle's position is defined by a cubic polynomial, what characterizes its jerk?
cards.backInfo: The jerk of a particle with a cubic position function will be a constant value.

cards.info: What are the standard units for jerk if position is in meters and time is in seconds?
cards.backInfo: The units for jerk are meters per second cubed (m/s³).

cards.info: If $g(x) = f'(x)$, how is $f''(x)$ expressed in terms of $g(x)$?
cards.backInfo: $f''(x)$ is the first derivative of $g(x)$, or $g'(x)$.

cards.info: What is the general procedure for finding the fourth derivative, $f^{(4)}(x)$, of a function?
cards.backInfo: Differentiate the function four times sequentially, applying standard differentiation rules at each step.

cards.info: How is acceleration $a(t)$ related to velocity $v(t)$ in the derivative hierarchy?
cards.backInfo: Acceleration is the first derivative of velocity, $a(t) = v'(t)$.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A linear sequence showing the progression from position to jerk via differentiation.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/57543f47-142a-428d-a83e-914b337bc3ac-1786519342215-423.webp)

cards.info: In terms of acceleration $a(t)$, how is jerk $j(t)$ defined?
cards.backInfo: Jerk is the first derivative of acceleration, $j(t) = a'(t)$.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A linear sequence showing the progression from position to jerk via differentiation.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/57543f47-142a-428d-a83e-914b337bc3ac-1786519342215-423.webp)

cards.info: If position is in feet and time in seconds, what are the units for acceleration?
cards.backInfo: The units are feet per second squared (ft/s²).

cards.info: Can a particle have a non-zero acceleration at a point where its velocity graph has a root?
cards.backInfo: Yes; acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph, which can be non-zero at a root.

cards.info: If $f''(x) > 0$ on an interval, what is happening to the slope of $f(x)$?
cards.backInfo: The slope of $f(x)$, which is $f'(x)$, is increasing on that interval.

cards.info: When using a table of $f'(x)$ values, why is the symmetric difference quotient preferred for $f''(a)$?
cards.backInfo: It provides a more accurate finite-difference estimate of the derivative at the midpoint $a$.

cards.info: Identify the error in this notation for the second derivative: $\frac{dy^2}{dx^2}$.
cards.backInfo: The '2' should be placed after the 'd' in the numerator: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$.

cards.info: If $p(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d$, what is the value of $p'''(t)$?
cards.backInfo: The third derivative (jerk) is the constant $6a$.
